conclusion.justification: The report concludes that the evidence regarding ginkgo extract for tinnitus is mixed, inconclusive, and uncertain, pointing to both positive trials and negative Cochrane reviews without taking a definitive stance. Therefore, it is best categorized as hedged.
conclusion.label: hedged

report:
The evidence on whether ginkgo extract relieves tinnitus symptoms is **mixed and inconclusive**, so a simple "yes" is not well supported by the highest-quality evidence.

**Positive evidence:** A systematic review of randomized, placebo-controlled trials concluded that EGb 761®, a standardized Ginkgo biloba extract, is an "evidence-based treatment option in tinnitus," noting that eight trials showed statistically significant benefits over placebo (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21857784/). An older multicenter double-blind study also reported conclusive effectiveness (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-73686-5_27).

**Negative/uncertain evidence:** The most authoritative assessment—the 2022 Cochrane systematic review (Sereda et al.), covering 12 RCTs with 1,915 participants—concluded there is "uncertainty about the benefits and harms of Ginkgo biloba for the treatment of tinnitus when compared to placebo," with high or unclear risk of bias across studies (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD013514_ginkgo-biloba-herbal-supplement-tinnitus). An earlier Cochrane review similarly found no demonstrated benefit (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003852_ginkgo-biloba-tinnitus). A 2004 BMJ trial and other clinical sources also found no effectiveness for tinnitus as a primary complaint (https://boards.straightdope.com/t/tinnitus-from-menieres-got-lipoflavonoid/633744).

**Bottom line:** While some standardized extracts (particularly EGb 761®) show promise in selected trials, the overall body of evidence—especially the Cochrane reviews—does not reliably demonstrate that ginkgo extract relieves tinnitus symptoms beyond placebo. The answer is closer to "uncertain" than a confident "yes."
